assets.title: 1. Medir y sujetar el hierro
assets.prompt:
Use case: ui-mockup. Asset type: ONE high quality landscape 16:9 GAMEPLAY CONCEPT SCREEN for a redesigned six-step interactive pixel-art ironworking workshop, preview only. Input image is a STYLE and CONTINUITY REFERENCE of the current game, not a fixed layout. Create a visibly improved playable scene, not a retouched screenshot. Preserve warm detailed pixel-art dark soot brick, plain riveted machinery, amber furnace glow, worn oak and modest antique brass interface. Crisp intentional pixel clusters and legible silhouettes, not photorealism or smooth digital painting. Tools must look like tangible textured pixel-art sprites, not rectangles/circles from primitive graphics. High quality close-up mechanics, all believable and connected, same perspective. No people, hands, modern electric motors, neon digital widgets, mouse cursors, tutorial arrows or dashed instructional diagrams.
Layout: refined thin wood-and-brass outer frame. Slim top strip has the exact Spanish phase title at upper left, small ordinary dark inventory HUD at upper right reading "77   Inventario", then one short instruction beneath the title. Optional six tiny step medallions centered at top, current one highlighted. Usable MAIN WORKSHOP is at least 85% of the image, extends almost the full width; REMOVE reference's entire right-hand essay sidebar and entire row of generic action buttons. Frame bottom contains only small "Volver" at left and a short context hint at center, with one optional small "Comprobar" button at far right. Tool interactions should be communicated by the physical scene, subtle warm outline on ONE selected tool and one unobtrusive short prompt attached to it. All Spanish text exact and concise, no invented tiny illegible paragraphs. The scene is an aspirational gameplay still: depict the proposed action in progress. Do not promise animation through printed diagrams or multiple-panel montages.
Text (verbatim): title "1. Medir y sujetar el hierro". Subtitle "Mide la barra y fíjala entre las mordazas.". Footer "Arrastra herramientas · Gira las mordazas".
Scene: a broad close-up worn oak workbench, foundry machinery receding softly behind. At center an oblique horizontal medium rectangular COLD solid iron billet is secured in a tangible iron bench vise with two independent brass-ended horizontal screw clamps, substantial and proportionate. A real wooden measuring rule lies aligned alongside the billet; a brass SLIDING-JAW caliper actually straddles the billet's thickness, jaws visibly moveable, one selected grip subtly outlined. At upper left tabletop a small parchment WORK ORDER shows only an ink connecting-rod silhouette and two dimension lines, not a wall of numbers. On the lower-left tray lie two alternative billets (one short thick, one overly thin), visibly different proportions, with NO answer labels such as correct or wrong and no colored answer glow. At right a piece of chalk and snug wood length-stop gauge. Prioritize actual measurement, comparing blueprint and securing both clamps. Small physical prompt "Girar mordaza". Scene should feel like an object manipulation puzzle from a wheelwright workshop, rather than a choice quiz.

Text (verbatim): title "2. Repartir el calor". Subtitle "Mueve el hierro hasta que su color sea uniforme.". Footer "Tenazas: mover hierro · Volante: regular aire".
Scene: industrial BRICK REHEATING HEARTH at left-center, not a melting pot. Solid rectangular iron bar stretches horizontally partially inside the hearth, supported on its firebrick lip. Long real iron tongs firmly grip its cool near end and extend out toward the foreground right, with handles accessible and NO hands. The same solid bar shows a subtle continuous heating gradient from dark red near the tongs to orange toward the fire; its shape remains intact, absolutely no molten liquid or droplets. Flame curls, little embers and heat shimmer suggest response to air. On the right, a strongly readable period air-control wheel connected to a mechanical damper and blower pipe; wheel grip is the sole highlighted interaction, unobtrusive prompt "Regular aire". On the near ledge a little mounted ceramic reference card with three iron-color swatches dark red / warm orange / pale yellow, center orange framed brass, no modern percentage bar or thermometer. Composition makes it obvious that moving the bar WITH the tongs distributes heat and the control wheel varies the fire. No extra controls, no inventory coal payment.

Scene: full imposing but proportionate steam-hammer machine, twin uprights and cylinder above, square heavy moving hammer head at the low point of a real stroke, aligned with the work on the anvil. On the anvil lies a hot ORANGE SOLID wrought-iron blank in the early process of becoming a connecting rod: a thick forged small left end already emerging, a still roughly rectangular hot neck, and a chunky larger right end NOT YET SHAPED. NO HOLES in either end, no perfect finished rod before work. The die block immediately under the active part has a physical neck-channel recess. Three real interchangeable dark iron die blocks lie in an inset foreground rack, each with a clearly different small rounded / flat neck / large rounded recess. Long iron tongs hold the blank, extending safely off to the side; a carriage with three physical stops guides its left-right positions. At right of machine, tall wooden-handled lever with pivot and linkage, physically connected to valve mechanism; subtly selected handle, small prompt "Bajar palanca". Tiny bright sparks and black scale chips at the impact, slight local deformation visible. Small wood pattern of the target SOLID rod shape propped behind the dies. Emphasize manipulating dies, sliding the iron, and pulling a real lever rather than hotkeys or hit counters. No printed progress words on top of the iron.

Text (verbatim): title "6. Probar con la manivela". Subtitle "Monta la biela y completa tres vueltas suaves.". Footer "Gira la manivela · Ajusta el freno si hace falta".
Scene: a convincing SMALL tabletop TRANSMISSION TEST RIG on oak bench, centered and occupying most usable area. A horizontal cylinder/piston housing at LEFT sends a sliding polished piston rod along a visible straight guide to a SMALL connecting-rod left eye. Connecting rod slender SOLID neck runs to LARGER right eye pinned to an ECCENTRIC crank point on the face of a moderately sized six-spoke iron flywheel at RIGHT. Both eyes have matching correctly centered brass pin caps with retaining cotters. EVERYTHING at coherent believable scale and consistent raised frontal perspective; connecting rod must be narrow relative to wheel and not a huge floating overlay, piston and linkage actually CONNECT, flywheel axle sits on bolted bearing stand, rod must not be fixed at the wheel center. A visible wooden-handled MANUAL CRANK projects from flywheel face for pointer circular turning, the handle subtly outlined, small prompt "Girar a mano". At flywheel rim a simple leather-band friction brake with small wooden-handled adjustment lever adds a light load, mounted on the same base and connected. At front base three small physical brass proof flags, first two raised and third down, show three turns without a digital countdown. Tiny short paper strip on a side roller shows repetitive stroke marks as a teaching visualization of motion. Tray with an optional spare pin, no duplicate unmounted biela if installed. No self-driving steam plume, no five-second progress bar; this is hand-driven validation of the assembled mechanism.
